html:
The relationship between basal-ganglia and cortical plasticity is best understood not as a contrast between two wholly different learning principles, but as a contrast between two parameterizations of the same broad three-factor logic deployed for different computational purposes. In both systems, recent pre- and postsynaptic coactivity can write an eligibility-like state that is later converted into lasting synaptic change by additional modulatory or circuit-level signals. But the function of that machinery differs. In cortex, plasticity is comparatively more heterogeneous, compartmentalized, and partly self-supervised: dendritic voltage landscapes, local calcium dynamics, disinhibitory motifs, homeostatic constraints, and longer eligibility windows allow cortical circuits to refine predictive features, latent causes, and internal world models across multiple timescales. In the basal ganglia, by contrast, the same generic primitives are tuned toward evaluative policy updating: eligibility windows are shorter, dependence on phasic dopamine is stronger, and opponent D1/D2 pathway rules translate scalar outcome information into selective strengthening or weakening of action-linked representations 1, 2, 3, 4. The cortex therefore tends to learn what is there and what it means; the basal ganglia tend to learn what to do about it. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Yet these systems are inseparable in operation, because each trains under conditions partly created by the other. Cortical populations provide the high-dimensional state, context, and action representations that converge onto SPN spines and become eligible for dopaminergic credit assignment; basal-ganglia output, in turn, biases thalamocortical traffic, action selection, exploration, and the statistics from which cortex learns. Empirically, skill learning is accompanied by coordinated plasticity across both structures rather than isolated modification in either one alone: corticostriatal plasticity is required for abstract skill learning, corticostriatal coherence and offline coupling increase with practice, and motor learning strengthens the outputs of motor-cortex engram neurons onto striatal SPNs; conversely, direct- and indirect-pathway manipulations can reshape cortical activity and perceptual representations, while motor-cortical and thalamic inputs to striatum make dissociable contributions to acquisition and execution 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. The most useful synthesis, then, is that cortex and basal ganglia form a nested optimizer pair: cortex learns the representational geometry of the task, whereas the basal ganglia learn which cortical representations should be gated, repeated, suppressed, or consolidated into policy. BG plasticity is thus not an alternative to cortical plasticity, but the evaluative counterpart that closes the loop between world-model construction and action selection. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).
